claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi can exist as a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The relevant initial CoCrFeMnNi state is coarse-grained rather than ultrafine-grained.
Sliding produces intense near-surface plastic deformation in the alloy.
Sliding dynamically forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The dynamically transformed layer may be partially amorphous.
The transformed surface layer absorbs mechanical energy.
The transformed layer reduces wear by accommodating shear.
The transformed layer acts as a passivating barrier that limits transport of corrosive species.
Formation of the transformed layer reduces corrosion rates during tribo-corrosion.
A single dynamic surface transformation governs both mechanical wear and electrochemical corrosion under tribo-corrosion.
Specimens that form the transformed layer will have lower total degradation than specimens in which the transformation is inhibited or absent.
Specimens that form the transformed layer will have lower wear rates than a matched transformation-suppressed baseline.
Specimens that form the transformed layer will have lower corrosion current densities than a matched transformation-suppressed baseline.
Pre-annealing can suppress dynamic surface grain refinement or amorphization.
Compositional modification can suppress dynamic surface grain refinement or amorphization.
The transformation requires a sufficiently high mechanical energy input or load.
An aggressive corrosion environment can destroy or rapidly oxidize the nascent transformed layer and eliminate its protection.
Testing in an inert environment provides a baseline in which the beneficial ultra-nanocrystalline layer is absent.

contradictions.description: The controlled comparison is described as using identical electrolyte conditions, but the baseline alternatively permits an inert, non-corrosive environment. Changing the environment does not isolate formation of the transformed layer and is not a matched tribo-corrosion control.

The hypothesis attributes layer formation to mechanical sliding and deformation, whereas the baseline implies that an inert environment makes the layer absent. The cited inert-environment study instead reports formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer during sliding.
